extracted.intended_audience: astronomers and mathematicians (readers of classical celestial mechanics; advanced students and researchers computing lunar motions and tides)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures, approximations, and formulae for computing the hourly, mean, and true motion of the Moon's nodes, the hourly and total variation of the Moon-orbit inclination, and the solar and lunar forces on the sea, with numerical examples and corrections (Newtonian/Principia-style geometric methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation: treat moon–sun lines as parallel to earth–sun lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider all lines drawn from the Moon to the Sun as parallel to the line drawn from the Earth to the Sun when computing nodal motions, because the orbital inclination effects are very small and complicate the calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to simplify calculations of nodal motion and to neglect minor inclination-induced effects when computing mediocris (mean) nodal motion. Quotation: 'considero lineas omnes à Luna ad Solem ductas tanquam parallelas lineæ quæ à Terra ad Solem ducitur, propterea quod inclinatio tantum ferè minuit effectus omnes ... & Nodorum motus mediocres quærimus, neglectis istiusmodi minutiis.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose solar perturbing force into transverse (3IT) and radial (PI) components; use transverse for node-plane perturbation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun's disturbing force on the Moon is decomposed into two parts: one proportional to 2IT (or 2Kp) and another proportional to PI; the radial component (PI) largely acts in the orbital plane and can be neglected for nodal-plane perturbation, while the transverse component composes with IT to give a total 3IT that perturbs the inclination/line of nodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decomposition justifies neglecting the in-plane component when computing the motion of the nodes: 'Et vis Solis ... duplex erit, altera lineæ 2IT vel 2Kp, altera lineæ PI proportionalis. ... Vis autem IT cum vi 2IT componit vim totam 3IT, qua planum Orbis Lunaris perturbatur.' Use the transverse 3IT (or appropriate scaled quantity) as the perturbing force for nodal motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local nodal velocity proportional to product of specific lengths/sines (IT × PH × sin STN etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a small displacement, the instantaneous angular velocity of the nodes is proportional to the product of the transverse disturbing length (IT), the perpendicular PH, and sin(STN) — equivalently expressed as the content under the sines of three angles TPI, PTN & STN.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived geometric relation: 'Est igitur velocitas Nodorum ut IT × PH & Sinus anguli STN conjunctim, sive ut contentum sub sinubus trium angulorum TPI, PTN & STN.' Use this proportionality as the basis for computing nodal hourly motion in the circular-orbit approximation; plug in the appropriate geometric quantities to get numeric values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign rule: when an angle's sign flips, nodal motion reverses (regressive ↔ progressive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the sign of a relevant angle changes from positive to negative or vice versa, the nodal motion changes sign: retrograde (regressivus) becomes prograde (progressivus) and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in piecewise computations across orbital sectors: 'Et quoties signum anguli alicujus de affirmativo in negativum, deque negativo in affirmativum mutatur, debebit motus regressivus in progressivum & progressivus in regressivum mutari.' Use this rule when assembling nodal motion over arcs where geometric signs change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX — Hourly motion of lunar nodes in a circular orbit
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to find the hourly motion of the Moon's nodes assuming the Moon moves in a circular orbit about the Earth: join geometric displacements, drop perpendiculars to the ecliptic, relate the small plane-tilting displacement to chordal/area ratios, and deduce nodal angular velocity as proportional to IT × PH and sin(STN) (or the product of sines of three angles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed geometric construction given; in the special case when the three angles (TPI, PTN, STN) are right (i.e., nodes at quadrature and Moon at syzygy), the derived hourly nodal motion is computed numerically: e.g., motus horarius Nodorum (in that case) ≈ 33" 10' 33"''' 12^v (text's tabulated sexagesimal notation). Use the geometric construction and proportionality to compute hourly nodal motion for arbitrary positions; include the sign-change rule above when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. XXX: nodal motion ∝ area × (AZ)^2 and relation to mean hourly motion in syzygies
rubrics_metrics.description: If from the arc PM one draws perpendiculars to the quadrature-line etc., the hourly nodal motion is proportional to the area MPDd and the square of the line AZ (i.e., product PK × PH × AZ). In the given configuration the mean hourly motion is half the hourly motion in syzygies; numerical mean values are provided (e.g., 16" 35' 16"''' 36^v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the stated proportionality when computing nodal motion from small-area elements: 'erit motus horarius N. ut area MPDd & quadratum lineæ AZ conjunctim.' Corollary gives practical mean-hourly numbers used later in averaging and annual sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI — Hourly nodal motion in an elliptical lunar orbit: scale circular result by ellipse/circle area ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Moon moves on an ellipse, the nodal motion corresponding to the same small-time arc is proportional to the area pDdm described in the ellipse; the nodal motion in the ellipse is to that in the circle as the ellipse's area (or circumference/area ratio) to the circle's — concretely as the ellipse semidiameter ratio (Ta to TA, numerically 68-11/12 : 69-11/12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses tangent similarity and area-comparison arguments: 'motus Nodorum in Ellipsi ut area pDdm.' Consequently, mean nodal motions in the elliptic case are obtained by multiplying the circular-case value by the ellipse/circle ratio (given numerically in the text). Use this when correcting circular-orbit nodal rates to elliptical-orbit rates; later numeric corrected mean hourly nodal motion is given (e.g., 16" 21' 2"''' 36^v).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment for lunar-area-driven time variation: account for syzygy/quadrature area differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Moon describes area faster in syzygies than in quadratures, times in syzygies are contracted and in quadratures extended; nodal motion (computed per equal arc subdivisions of the orbit) therefore accelerates or retards in a doubled ratio of the time change. This produces corrections to the nodal mean motion that are proportional to combinations of numbers 10973, 11073, and their semi-sums/semi-differences (text's numerical bookkeeping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply correction factors derived from the ratios of area momenta (e.g., momentum in quadratures : in syzygies = 10973 : 11073) to compute increments/decrements to nodal motion across octants/quadrants; use the provided numeric manipulations to obtain corrected mediocris values (text gives step-by-step numeric reductions leading to corrected mediocris hourly motion ≈ 16" 16' 36"''' 48^v).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXII — Compute the mean (annual) motion of the nodes by integrating hourly mean motions over the year (area method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual mean motion of the nodes equals the sum of all hourly mean motions over the year, which can be obtained by integrating the product AZ × ZY (areas AZYa), so that the sum of hourly means is proportional to the area NAZ; compare maxima and totals using circle/rectangle area relations to derive numeric annual motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: take AZq as measure of hourly mean (ob proportional AZ, ZY) and sum across the circle; use area relations (sum of many small rectangles vs total circle area) to show the maximum-hourly value corresponds to a specific number (16" 16' 36"''' 48^v etc.), and compute the annual nodal motion (e.g., results in mean annual nodal motion ≈ 19° 18' 0".22"' ). Includes correction for nodal motion shortening the solar return, and a series-method numeric integral producing corrections (area of figure NeFnT ≈ 0.1188478 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII — Compute the true nodal motion via a geometric construction (annual equation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain the true (actual) motion of the nodes rather than the mean, construct a corrective geometric device: draw a circle BEFD centered at C with interval CD, extend DC to A so that AB:AC = mean motion : half the true mean, draw tangent Gg at D, take angles proportional to twice the distance of the nodes from quadratures, and use the tangents and perpendicularly cut lengths to add a correction to the mean nodal motion. The correction yields the annual equation and a monthly equation (the latter less important for lunar latitude computations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constructed correction produces the 'true' nodal motion which closely matches the area method's exact result (NTA - NdZ formula). Corollary: nodes are stationary in syzygies and regress in quadratures with hourly regression ~16" 18' 41"''' ½; the equation in octants ≈ 1°30'. Use the geometric construction and add the computed angle to the mean to get the true nodal motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIV — Hourly variation of inclination of the lunar orbit to the ecliptic (formulaic proportionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The instantaneous hourly variation (GPg) of the lunar orbit's inclination is proportional to a product of geometric quantities involving the perturbing transverse length IT, AZ, TG, and the sine of the inclination (Pp/PG), scaled by AT cubed. Specifically GPg : 33"10'33"''' :: IT × AZ × TG × Pp ÷ PG : AT^3 (per the construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a working formula to compute the small hourly change of orbital inclination due to solar perturbation; corollaries show how to integrate these hourly variations over a month or octant to get monthly/total inclination variations. Use the provided proportional form and numerical constants (33"10'33"''' as reference angle) to compute GPg for a given configuration. The total variation over the transit from quadrature to syzygy (177 1/6 hours) integrates to ≈ 164" (≈ 2'44").

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. XXXIV: integrate hourly variations to get monthly/total inclination changes and link to nodal distances
rubrics_metrics.description: If one sums/integrates hourly inclination variations while the nodes and Earth are moving, the total monthly variation is proportional to the aggregate of the generated small areas (HpMh etc.) scaled by AZ × TZ × Pp ÷ PG over AT^3. In special positions (nodes at quadrature vs syzygy) specific numerical totals and ratios are derived (e.g., total variation ≈ 2'44", half/adjusted depending on node positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the corollaries' area-aggregation method to compute total inclination change during a transition (quadrature→syzygy) and to obtain the mediocris hourly variation for given nodal configurations. The derivations give practical numbers: e.g., when inclination ≈ 5°2', the total variation computed is 164" (2'44"); adjustments when nodes are in syzygy add/subtract ~2'44" producing recorded observational values close to 5° or 5°17'½ as reported by astronomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXV — Given time, construct the inclination (geometric construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometric construction to find the Moon-orbit inclination at a given time: take AD = sine of max inclination, AB = sine of min inclination, bisect BD at C, draw circle of radius BC centered at C; take CE on AC in the ratio of EB to 2BA, construct angle AEG equal to twice the nodal distance from quadrature at the given time and drop perpendicular GH; then AH is the sine of the desired inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes a specific ruler-and-circle geometric method to obtain the instantaneous inclination (sine); includes algebraic identities showing GE^2 relates to AH and how the construction preserves the sinusoidal dependence. Use this construction when a direct analytic computation is inconvenient; the proposition also shows how to adjust for small nonuniformities and gives numeric examples of total variations (e.g., maximum variation ≈16'24").

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium: apogee motion remarks and caution about table inaccuracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations and calculations indicate the lunar apogee's motion is progressive by about 23" per day (when in conjunction/opposition) and regressive about 16 1/3" per day (when in quadratures), giving an annual mean near 40°; published tables (e.g., adapted by Flamsteed to Horrox's hypothesis) show slightly different numbers, and some discrepancies likely arise from tabular errors and the complexity of the computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the calculated progressive/regressive daily motions as rough checks against tabled values; exercise caution about trusting existing astronomical tables without cross-checking, because small approximation choices and neglected complexities (excentricity, inclination) can shift tabulated rates by minutes of arc per day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVI — Compute the Sun's tidal force on the seas via gravitational ratio and distance scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun's perturbing tidal effect (in quadratures) relative to local gravity at Earth's surface is approximately 1 : 38,604,600 (after scaling to Earth's surface from the earlier Perturbation estimate of 1 : 638,092.6 at Earth's center and a distance drop factor ≈60½). The component that depresses sea level at regions 90° from the Sun and the component that elevates it under the Sun/opposite sum to a net solar tidal potential equal to a specified fraction of gravity (1 : 12,868,200).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the solar tidal effect by scaling the perturbing force by the inverse-square-like distance factor from Earth's center to surface (60.5 : 1 given), then combine the depression/elevation contributions appropriately (doubling or differencing depending on configuration). Use the derived ratio to estimate water-level differences; the corollary shows that relative to the centrifugal effect producing ~85,200 Paris feet equatorial excess, the solar tide produces only ~1 Paris foot + 11 digits difference between sunlit/opposite and 90° positions (approximate small magnitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVII — Infer the Moon's tidal force from observed tide heights and compute lunar-to-solar force ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the Moon's perturbing force relative to the Sun's by using observed tide heights at specified locations (e.g., Avon near Bristol, and Plymouth) and accounting for declination effects (sinus complement scaling). Using these observational constraints, derive L : S (lunar to solar force) — Newton obtains several ratios from different data and adopts an intermediate value ~6 1/3 : 1 — giving lunar force relative to gravity ≈ 1 : 2,031,821.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: model observed rise in conjunction/opposition vs quadrature as arising from L+S and (0.841)L - S (0.841 = squared sin complementary due to declination ~23½°), solve for L/S with tide-height ratios (e.g., 45:25 at Avon). Several observed datasets give slightly different ratios (5-7/15:1, 7-1/3:1, etc.); adopt median ~6 1/3:1 until better observations exist. Corollary: with the adopted ratio, lunar tidal force would raise water to about 12 feet under typical equatorial assumptions; textual discussion explains why tidal amplitude varies with ocean width, depth, local geometry, and resonance (e.g., larger tides in Pacific due to width and depth). Use observationally-constrained inversion to estimate lunar tidal magnitude rather than purely theoretical ratios.
